land.text: the Jawf valley around Qarnawu (Ma'in) and Baraqish, Cliopatria's Minaean shape of 383-189 BCE: the Sabaeans regained control over Ma'in 'after the collapse of Qataban in 50 BC'

successors.note: History of Yemen page. Cliopatria instead hands the whole 214,510 km2 Minaean footprint to the Himyarite Kingdom from -66 (its shape 'himyarite-kingdom_-66' is 334,765 km2 and its -36 shape is the same 214,510 km2 as the last Minaean shape); the Minaeans page puts the demise in the 1st century CE as the most popular hypothesis. The northern caravan-road land is handed to nobody (the pages name no taker).

capitals.name: Qarnawu (Ma'in) and Baraqish, Wadi al-Jawf
capitals.note: Minaeans page: 'a city-state settled in the town of Qarnawu (modern-day Jawf)'; 'The kingdom of Ma'in in this time was mainly based on an alliance between two cities: Ma'in and Baraqish.' History of Yemen page puts the capital at Baraqish. Neither page dates a move, and the two towns lie in the same valley, so one entry carries both. The page gives no coordinates: lon/lat are the centre of the Jawf core region (Al Jawf governorate inside Cliopatria's Minaean shape); a gap-filler should replace them with the gazetteer's Qarnawu/Baraqish.

correction.text: the Jawf valley around Qarnawu (Ma'in) and Baraqish: 'a city-state settled in the town of Qarnawu (modern-day Jawf)'; the page gives no boundary, so this is Cliopatria's first Minaean shape cut to the Al Jawf governorate

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's Minaeans begin in -383 with 28,484 km2 but the page has the 'transition from a city-state to kingdom in the last quarter of the 7th century BCE'. Nashshan, 'the most important city of the Jawf valley', 'was absorbed under the dominion of the Kingdom of Ma'in between the 6th and 4th centuries BC', so before the absorption the kingdom is drawn as the core only (6,300 km2 of cells). Extent is the researcher's reading (page silent on borders). The Sabaean dossier holds the whole Jawf until -383.

28,484 km2 (bbox 15.9-17.8 N, 42.5-45.2 E): the northern Jawf with Nashshan, Yathill and the Raghwan towns. Sabaeans page: some former Sabaean towns were 'absorbed into Ma'in', including Yathill and the towns of Wadhi Raghwan; Minaeans page: Nashshan absorbed 'between the 6th and 4th centuries BC'. Neither page gives the year, so -383 (Cliopatria's) stands. The Minaeans infobox gives no area; no comparison possible. The shape reaches 42.5 E, west of the Wadi al-Jawf the page names: an envelope, not a survey.

137,480 km2 reaching 21.2 N: the caravan road north of the Jawf. Minaeans page: 'Ma'in also took control over the commercial caravan route along the Red Sea (from the Hijaz, to Dedan, to the Mediterranean Sea)' - undated. Unverified for the year (page silent). The road is a line of stations and tribes, not solid territory: draw soft.

214,403 km2 reaching 26.4 N (Dedan/al-Ula, 38.2 E). History of Yemen: by the 3rd century BC Ma'in 'became independent from Saba', its rule reached as far as Dedan, capital Baraqish (paraphrase); Lihyan page: Dedan 'hosted a community of Minaeans'. The pages date the reach to the 3rd century BC or earlier, not to -170; the year stands as Cliopatria's. The Dedan end is a trade colony inside Lihyan's town, drawn here as territory by Cliopatria.

correction.text: the shape unchanged, with its years extended from -67 to -51: the Sabaeans regained control over Ma'in 'after the collapse of Qataban in 50 BC', so Ma'in is Minaean until then; Cliopatria has no Minaean shape for -66..-37

keyframe_review.note: 214,510 km2 (within 107 km2 of the preceding shape). Cliopatria ends it in -67 and resumes with a different shape in -36; the only page that dates the end (History of Yemen, 50 BC) gives -50 for the Sabaean recovery. The Minaeans page prefers the 1st century CE as the demise ('the most popular hypothesis'). No infobox area to compare.

correction.text: no Minaean shape: the dossier ends in -50. The only Minaean land the pages tie to these years is the Jawf, now Sabaean again (the Sabaeans regained control over Ma'in 'after the collapse of Qataban in 50 BC'); Cliopatria's Sabaean shape of -31..-26 (54,376 km2, to 17.8 N) covers it

keyframe_review.note: 84,538 km2 at 12.6-15.5 N, 42.9-46.6 E: the south-western highlands, with the same box as Cliopatria's Himyarite shape of -25..-20 (84,904 km2), not the Jawf (15.9-17.8 N) where Ma'in stood. A mislabelled Himyarite row. The Minaean state ended in -50 in this dossier.

correction.text: no Minaean shape (same reading as minaeans_-36): the Jawf is Sabaean land after -50

keyframe_review.note: Same 84,538 km2 south-western footprint as minaeans_-36, for -27..-26; see that verdict.

region.text: the Jawf valley around Qarnawu (Ma'in) and Baraqish

ledger.note: c. 625 BCE: Ma'in becomes a kingdom in the Jawf. 'transition from a city-state to kingdom in the last quarter of the 7th century BCE' (page); the city-state at Qarnawu is already in the record 'in the 8th century BCE'. -625 is the first year of that quarter, a reading of the page's span. The territory is not described; the core is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Nashshan, 'the most important city of the Jawf valley', Yathill and the Wadhi Raghwan towns: the rest of Cliopatria's first Minaean shape

ledger.note: By -383 the north of the Jawf passes to Ma'in. Some former Sabaean towns were 'absorbed into Ma'in', including Yathill and the Raghwan towns, after Karib'il Watar's successors failed to hold the Jawf (Sabaeans page); Minaeans page: Nashshan 'was absorbed under the dominion of the Kingdom of Ma'in between the 6th and 4th centuries BC'. Neither page gives the year; -383 is Cliopatria's shape year (confidence 1). The Sabaean dossier carries the matching loss.

region.text: the caravan road north of the Jawf towards the Hijaz, as far as the Najran and Asir highlands (21.2 N)

ledger.note: -188: Ma'in controls the incense road to the north. 'Ma'in also took control over the commercial caravan route along the Red Sea (from the Hijaz, to Dedan, to the Mediterranean Sea)' (page, undated); -188 is Cliopatria's shape year, so the date is the researcher's bridge. The page has Ma'in take the route from Saba, but the road is a line of stations and no page or dossier gives Saba land north of the Jawf and Najran (the Sabaean shapes stop at 17.8 N), so the counterpart is nobody [reviewer me-04-c, 2026-10-19].

region.text: the road on to Dedan (al-'Ula), where Ma'in had a community in Lihyan's town

ledger.note: -170: the Minaean reach extends to Dedan. History of Yemen: Ma'in 'became independent from Saba' by the 3rd century BC and its rule reached as far as Dedan (paraphrase); Lihyan page: Dedan 'hosted a community of Minaeans', no date, no conquest. The year is Cliopatria's shape year; the pages describe a trade colony in Lihyan's town, not a taking of Lihyan's land, so Lihyan's loss is doubtful. Lihyan has no dossier yet.

region.text: the Jawf valley around Qarnawu (Ma'in) and Baraqish

ledger.note: -50: Saba takes Ma'in back. History of Yemen: the Sabaeans regained control over Ma'in 'after the collapse of Qataban in 50 BC' (paraphrase around the quoted fragment). The Qataban page dates Qataban's end to the late 1st or late 2nd century CE, so the 50 BC 'collapse' is not Qataban's final end; the Sabaean dossier has the matching gain at -50.

region.text: the caravan road north of the Jawf to Dedan

ledger.note: -50: the northern road leaves the state. 'After the collapse of the Minaeans, the Nabataean Kingdom took over long-distance trade in the region' (page, undated); Lihyan page: Nabataean annexation of Lihyan 'around 24 BC' (Caskel) or about 65 BC with Dedan falling 9 BC. Trade, not territory: the pages name no taker for the land, so it goes to nobody (confidence 1).

region.text: the Minaean kingdom as last drawn: the Jawf with the caravan road to Dedan

ledger.note: -50: the Minaean kingdom ends. The Sabaeans regain Ma'in (History of Yemen, 50 BC); the Minaeans page says only that 'the most popular hypothesis places its demise in the 1st century CE', so the end year is the earlier of the two page statements.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey exists for any Minaean frontier: the Jawf valley is approximate (pages name only towns), and the caravan road to Dedan is a line of stations, never a border.

notes:
Page budget: 5 pages (Minaeans, Sabaeans, History of Yemen, Lihyan, Qataban). The Minaeans article is thin (no infobox area, no capital, no king dates), so most border events rest on Cliopatria's shape years at confidence 1.

Cliopatria rows: (1) the first shape starts in -383 but the page has the kingdom from the last quarter of the 7th century BCE: new keyframe -625..-384 for the Jawf core. (2) The -36 and -27 shapes (84,538 km2, 12.6-15.5 N) are the south-western highlands, the footprint of Cliopatria's Himyarite -25..-20 shape, not Minaean land: marked wrong. (3) Cliopatria has no Minaean shape for -66..-37 and gives the Minaean footprint (214,510 km2) to the Himyarite Kingdom from -66; this dossier extends the -164 shape to -51 and ends the state in -50 on the History of Yemen's date, handing the Jawf to the Sabaeans. The himyarite-kingdom dossier (me-06) should not keep the Minaean footprint for -66..-37 unless it finds a page for it.

Disagreements: end -50 (History of Yemen: Sabaeans regained Ma'in after 50 BC) against the Minaeans page's 'most popular hypothesis' of the 1st century CE; Ma'in 'became independent from Saba' by the 3rd century BC (History of Yemen) while the Minaeans page has the alliance with Saba breaking down about 600 BCE. The History of Yemen's 'collapse of Qataban in 50 BC' conflicts with the Qataban page (late 1st or late 2nd century CE).

Not settled (page silent): the Qatabanian conquest of Ma'in (Qataban page: 'was able to conquer Ma'in, and soon embarked on a successful expansionist policy against Sabaʾ' after its late-5th-century independence, no year; the king list notes 'Šahr Yagil ... (conquered Maʿīn)'). It is not in the ledger or wars because no page dates it and the Minaean shapes do not change; a gap-filler needs a Qatabanian source or Seshat. The Minaean trade colonies abroad (Egypt, Delos) are in the page as inscriptions only and are not territory.

Counterparts needing dossiers: Lihyan (Dedan/al-'Ula), counterpart of the -170 gain. Region names the gazetteer lacks (no region used needs one; place names for the capital dots): Qarnawu, Baraqish, Dedan (al-'Ula).
